title: The eagle-bearer of the Tenth
saying: Dēsilīte, mīlitēs, nisi vultis aquilam hostibus prōdere
author: Caesar
setting: The coast of Britain, late summer 55 BC

edition.name: Caesar, Selections from the Gallic War, ed. edition.section: Bellum Gallicum 4.25.3–5 (the page has paragraphs, not section numbers; sections as in T. Rice Holmes's Oxford text)

source_text: Atque nostris militibus cunctantibus, maxime propter altitudinem maris, qui decimae legionis aquilam ferebat, contestatus deos, ut ea res legioni feliciter eveniret, "Desilite", inquit, "milites, nisi vultis aquilam hostibus prodere; ego certe meum rei publicae atque imperatori officium praestitero." Hoc cum voce magna dixisset, se ex navi proiecit atque in hostes aquilam ferre coepit. Tum nostri cohortati inter se, ne tantum dedecus admitteretur, universi ex navi desiluerunt.
excerpt_note: Sections 3–5 of chapter 25 (the third and fourth paragraphs on the page, without the last sentence, which is section 6). The DCC prints macrons and single quotation marks, with a space inside each opening mark; here the text is given without macrons, with ASCII double quotation marks and without those spaces.

macrons.note: Macrons are editorial, not part of any manuscript. The DCC text is macronized; here vowel quantities follow the app lexicon (Wheelock / DCC spellings) where the word is in it, and otherwise the DCC text. Where the DCC marks long vowels before -gn- or -x- (māgnā, māximē) that the app lexicon does not, the app's spelling is used.
uncertain: magnā, maximē: the DCC text prints māgnā and māximē; the app lexicon has magnus, so magnā follows it, and maximē is printed the same way.
contestātus, cohortātī: long ā of the participle; as in the DCC, not machine-checked.
dēsiluērunt, Dēsilīte: long ē in dē-, as in the DCC; not machine-checked.

tokens.parse: relative pronoun, nom. sg. m. (antecedent understood: "the man who")
conjunction (noun clause of prayer after contestātus deōs)

tokens.gloss: I shall have done, will have performed

tokens.parse: nom. pl. m., used as a noun
conjunction (indirect command after cohortātī inter sē)

translation: And as our soldiers hung back, chiefly because the water was deep, the man who carried the eagle of the Tenth Legion called on the gods to let his act turn out well for the legion and cried, "Jump down, soldiers, unless you want to hand the eagle over to the enemy. I at any rate will have done my duty to the state and to my commander." When he had said this in a loud voice, he flung himself from the ship and began to carry the eagle toward the enemy. Then our men urged one another not to allow so great a disgrace, and all of them leapt down from the ship.
translation_note: quī ... ferēbat has no expressed antecedent: "(the man) who carried". praestiterō is a future perfect: "I shall have done my duty", whatever you do. ut ea rēs ... ēvenīret is a noun clause of prayer after contestātus deōs, and nē ... admitterētur an indirect command after cohortātī inter sē ("urged one another not to allow"). T. Rice Holmes's Oxford text (1914) reads X legionis aquilam gerebat and obtestatus where the DCC has decimae legionis aquilam ferebat and contestatus; the meaning is the same.

essay.t: With little of the summer left, Caesar crossed from Gaul to Britain, saying that the Britons had sent help to his enemies in almost all his Gallic wars.
He brought two legions in about eighty transports, with eighteen more ships assigned to the cavalry.

The landing went badly: the big ships could ride only in deep water, so soldiers weighed down with armour, on unfamiliar ground, had to jump into the waves and fight at once, while the Britons threw weapons from dry land or the shallows.
Here Caesar brings on the eagle-bearer of the Tenth, who prays, makes a short speech and leaps; shame does the rest.
Caesar does not name him, and reports words he can hardly have heard exactly over the noise of a landing.
Even the wording varies: the DCC text has decimae ... ferebat and contestatus, while Holmes's Oxford edition prints X legionis aquilam gerebat and obtestatus.
Once ashore, the Romans routed the Britons but could not pursue them, because the cavalry had not yet been able to reach the island; Caesar says this alone was missing from his usual good fortune.
Four days later a storm scattered the cavalry transports, and they never arrived.
With the equinox near and his ships damaged, he doubled his demand for hostages and sailed back to Gaul.
Yet when his dispatches reached Rome the senate decreed a thanksgiving of twenty days.
Britannica calls the expeditions of 55 and 54 BC brief raids that Western tradition has overestimated.
Caesar writes of himself in the third person ("Quod ubi Caesar animadvertit..." opens this chapter).
Britannica describes his commentaries as terse reports that look impersonal and objective, but in which every fact is selected so that readers see events in the light Caesar chooses.
Ancient readers already disagreed: Suetonius quotes Cicero praising their plain, unadorned style, and reports that Asinius Pollio thought them written with too little care and regard for truth.
The eagle-bearer's leap fits that pattern: a vivid scene that turns a near-disaster into a story of Roman courage.

questions.q: Why did the soldiers hesitate to leave the ships?
options: Chiefly because of the depth of the water
Because Caesar had ordered them to wait
Because the Britons had already surrendered
Because the eagle had fallen into the sea

questions.q: What did the senate decree after Caesar's dispatches arrived?
What did Asinius Pollio think of Caesar's commentaries, according to Suetonius?
options: That they were careless and not wholly true to the facts
That they were the finest history Rome had produced
That Hirtius, not Caesar, had really written them
That they were too ornate and full of rhetoric
